history.title: Check Before You Claim

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Bubbles are not proof. Neither is a colour change. This week you learn what actually counts as evidence that a new substance formed, and why mass that seems to disappear never really does.

1. Read **Did Anything New Actually Form?**
2. Learn the words in **Reaction Words**, then win the **Crossword**.
3. Study the **Signs and Their Impostors** chart — it is the heart of the unit.
4. Trace **What Happens to the Atoms** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Chemical or Physical?**
6. Take **Reaction Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Two Rules**.
8. Read **Reaction Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Investigation: The Sealed Bag**.

Your job this week: catch one claim — an advert, a video, a classmate — that treats a sign as if it were proof. ⚗️

history.title: Did Anything New Actually Form?
history.data:
## Did Anything New Actually Form?

Drop an antacid tablet in water and it fizzes furiously. Boil that same water and it bubbles just as hard. One of those is a chemical **reaction** and one is not. The bubbles cannot tell you which.

That is the problem this lesson solves.

A **substance** is a material with its own fixed **property** set: melting point, density, colour, how it reacts with other things. In a chemical reaction, the substances you start with — the **reactants** — are used up, and different substances — the **products** — appear in their place. In a **physical** change, no new substance appears. The same stuff has changed form.

Water boiling is physical. Steam is still water. Sugar dissolving is physical too, which surprises people, because the sugar vanishes from sight. Evaporate the water and the sugar comes back, unchanged. It was never destroyed, only spread out.

So what counts as evidence? Textbooks list five **indicators**: bubbles of gas, a colour change, a temperature change, light, and a **precipitate** — a solid appearing when two clear liquids mix.

Here is the part usually left out. **Every one of those five has a physical impostor.** Bubbles can be boiling. A colour change can be dilution. A temperature change can be dissolving, which warms or cools a solution without any reaction at all. Light can be an object glowing simply because it is hot. And a solid can appear because something merely suspended has settled out, with nothing new formed. Each indicator says *look closer*. None of them proves anything by itself.

The real test is the definition. Compare the properties before and after. If what you have at the end melts at a different temperature, or has a different density, or refuses to dissolve where the original dissolved easily, then you have different substances, and a reaction happened.

Now the second rule, and it is stranger.

Burn a log and the ash weighs far less than the wood. Mass looks lost. It is not. Carbon dioxide and water vapour left as gases, and nobody weighed them. Do the same burning inside a sealed container and the total mass does not budge.

That is because **atoms** are not created or destroyed in a reaction. They are rearranged. Every atom that goes in comes out, in some new arrangement, so mass is **conserved**. Antoine Lavoisier established this in the 1770s by insisting on sealed vessels and a good balance, which is a reminder that better measurement, not a better idea, settled it.

So ask two questions. Are the properties different now? And where did the atoms go?

sections.label: BUBBLES
bullets: Could be: a gas product forming
Impostor: water boiling, or dissolved gas escaping
Ask: is the gas a new substance?

sections.label: COLOUR CHANGE
bullets: Could be: a product with a different colour
Impostor: dilution, or two colours simply mixing
Ask: is the colour a new substance or a thinner one?

sections.label: TEMPERATURE CHANGE
bullets: Could be: energy released or absorbed by a reaction
Impostor: dissolving, which warms or cools with no reaction
sections.iconPrompt: a thermometer beside a stirred beaker

sections.label: LIGHT
bullets: Could be: energy released by a reaction
Impostor: an object glowing because it is hot
Ask: is anything new there once it cools?
sections.iconPrompt: a glowing hot metal rod held in tongs

sections.label: A PRECIPITATE
bullets: Could be: an insoluble product forming
Impostor: a solid settling out that was only suspended
The strongest of the five, still not proof
sections.iconPrompt: a cloudy solid forming where two clear liquids meet

sections.label: THE ACTUAL TEST
bullets: Different melting point, density, or solubility = different substance
Then ask where the atoms went

data.main: Atoms rearrange; nothing is created or destroyed

branches.title: Physical change: no new substance
items: Boiling water — steam is still water
Sugar dissolving — evaporate the water and the sugar returns unchanged
The same atoms, in the same groupings, arranged differently in space

branches.title: Chemical reaction: new substances
items: Reactants are used up; products appear in their place
The atoms are the same atoms, bonded into different groupings
Products have their own properties, not blends of the old ones

branches.title: Why mass seems to vanish
items: Burn a log: the ash weighs far less than the wood
Carbon dioxide and water vapour left as gases, unweighed
Do it in a sealed container and the total mass does not change

branches.title: Why mass is actually conserved
items: Every atom that goes in comes out
Counting atoms on both sides is what balancing an equation does
Lavoisier settled it in the 1770s with sealed vessels and a good balance

data.title: Remember the Two Rules
data.instructions: Two cards hold the reasoning. Study the example, build one of your own, then explain what it keeps you from getting wrong.
data.sourceExcerpt: Every one of those five has a physical impostor. Compare the properties before and after. Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction. They are rearranged.

cards.target: An indicator is a prompt to investigate, not proof
essentialFacts: The five indicators are bubbles, colour change, temperature change, light, and a precipitate.
Every one of them has a physical impostor.
The real test is comparing properties before and after.
cards.aiExample: SIGNS ARE SUSPECTS. A suspect is worth questioning and is not a conviction. Bubbles are a suspect. Boiling is the alibi. You convict on properties, not on appearance.
cards.mapping: Calling the indicators suspects keeps their real status: enough to start an investigation, never enough to close one.
cards.scaffoldStarter: ____ is a suspect. Its alibi is ____. I convict by ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick one of the five indicators.
Say what would actually settle it.
coachPrompts: Which of the five has the weakest alibi, and why?
cards.studentPrompt: Build your own phrase for what an indicator is worth.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Why is treating a sign as proof the most common mistake here?

history.title: Reaction Check

questions.question: A beaker of clear liquid starts bubbling. What have you established?
options: That a chemical reaction is definitely taking place
That a gas is being produced by new substances
That the liquid must have been an acid to begin with
That something is worth investigating, and nothing more
questions.correctAnswer: That something is worth investigating, and nothing more

questions.question: Which observation would best settle whether a reaction occurred?
options: The mixture became noticeably warmer while stirring
The solid left behind melts at a different temperature
The colour shifted from dark blue to a paler blue
Bubbles rose steadily from the bottom of the flask
questions.correctAnswer: The solid left behind melts at a different temperature

questions.question: Why is sugar dissolving in water a physical change?
options: Because the sugar can be recovered unchanged by evaporating
Because no bubbles or colour change happen while stirring
Because water is a liquid and sugar is a solid substance
Because the mixture does not get hot enough to react
questions.correctAnswer: Because the sugar can be recovered unchanged by evaporating

questions.question: Burning a log leaves ash weighing far less than the wood. Why is mass still conserved?
options: Some mass converts into the heat and light given off
Mass is only conserved in reactions that stay sealed
Gases left the system and were never put on the balance
The ash is denser, so the balance reading misleads you
questions.correctAnswer: Gases left the system and were never put on the balance

questions.question: What actually happens to atoms during a chemical reaction?
options: Some are destroyed and replaced by different atoms
They are rearranged into different groupings, none lost
They are compressed, which is why products weigh less
New atoms form from the energy released by the change
questions.correctAnswer: They are rearranged into different groupings, none lost

questions.question: A classmate mixes two liquids, sees the beaker get warm, and writes "a chemical reaction occurred." What is wrong with that reasoning, and what should they check?
questions.expectedAnswer: A temperature change is an indicator, not proof. Dissolving can warm or cool a solution with no reaction at all. They should compare the properties of what they have now with what they started with, such as melting point, density or solubility, and see whether a genuinely different substance is present.

questions.question: Design a way to show that mass is conserved when baking soda reacts with vinegar. Explain why your setup works.
questions.expectedAnswer: Carry out the reaction in a sealed container, such as a closed bag or a stoppered flask, and weigh it before and after. The mass stays the same because the carbon dioxide produced cannot escape and is still on the balance. Doing it in an open beaker would appear to lose mass, because the gas leaves unweighed.

reflections.text: Where have you seen a sign treated as proof, in science or anywhere else?
Which of the five indicators would fool you most easily, and why?

history.title: Reaction Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Is cooking a chemical change? 🍳
data.answer: Usually yes. A raw egg turning solid is proteins changing shape and bonding differently, and you cannot get the raw egg back. Melting butter, though, is physical. Cooking is a mix of both.

data.question: Does mass conservation hold in nuclear reactions?
data.answer: Not in the same simple way. In nuclear changes a tiny amount of mass converts to energy, which is what E = mc squared describes. For every chemical reaction you will meet in this course, mass is conserved.

data.question: Why does a cut apple go brown? 🍎
data.answer: Oxygen in the air reacts with compounds in the fruit, helped along by an enzyme released when you cut the cells open. It is a genuine chemical reaction, which is why lemon juice slows it down.

data.question: Can a reaction go backwards?
data.answer: Many can. Some run both ways at once and settle at a balance point. Others are practically one-way, like burning. Reversible does not mean easy to reverse.

data.question: Is dissolving really not a reaction? 🧂
data.answer: Usually not, and this trips up everyone. Salt in water separates into the charged particles it is built from, and evaporating brings the salt back unchanged. Some dissolvings do involve reactions, so the recovery test is the one to trust.

data.question: How did anyone prove atoms are conserved before they could see one?
data.answer: By weighing very carefully in sealed vessels. Lavoisier could not see an atom, but he could show that closed systems do not change mass. Good measurement settled it long before good microscopes existed.

history.meta: 6 questions • the nuclear one is the honest exception to the rule

history.title: Investigation: The Sealed Bag
history.meta: 8th Grade • Investigation brief • prove it, do not assert it

data.title: The Sealed Bag
data.instructions: Design and run a test that shows mass is conserved in a reaction that produces a gas. Then explain why an open beaker would have told you the opposite.
data.fitReason: MS-PS1-5 asks students to model conservation of mass. Running the same reaction open and sealed makes the apparent loss real and then makes it disappear, which is far more convincing than being told the atoms are still there.

brief.context: Your class has baking soda, vinegar, resealable bags, small beakers, a balance reading to 0.01 g, and safety glasses. Every group runs the reaction twice: once open and once sealed.
brief.audience: A group in the year below who have been told mass is conserved and do not believe it
brief.drivingQuestion: Does the total mass change when baking soda reacts with vinegar, and why do the open and sealed versions disagree?
brief.seedDirection: Weigh everything you are going to use, including the container and the lid, before you mix anything. If it will be on the balance at the end, it must be on the balance at the start.
lockedLessonFacts: Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction; they are rearranged.
Burning a log seems to lose mass because gases leave unweighed.
In a sealed container the total mass does not change.
An indicator such as bubbling is a prompt to investigate, not proof.
openQuestions: What exactly has to be on the balance for the measurement to be fair?
How much of a change would count as real, given how precise your balance is?
What would you predict if the bag leaked slightly?
stakeholders: The younger group who need convincing
Your lab partner, who records the masses
criteria: Masses recorded before and after for both the open and the sealed run
The procedure is written so another group could repeat it exactly
The difference in each run is compared against the balance's precision
The explanation accounts for the open result without abandoning conservation
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: Safety glasses on, bags not overfilled
No claim without a measurement behind it
brief.deliverable: A one-page report: your procedure, a table of masses for both runs, the difference in each, and a paragraph explaining to the younger group why the open beaker appeared to lose mass while nothing was actually lost.

parallelExample.context: A group found their sealed bag lost 0.03 g and wanted to declare conservation broken.
parallelExample.move: They checked their balance, which read to 0.01 g and drifted by about 0.02 g between weighings, and then noticed the bag had been squeezed. They resealed, repeated it three times, and the difference fell inside their measurement uncertainty.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: They compared the size of the difference to the precision of the instrument instead of treating any non-zero number as a result.

supports.frameStarter: In the open beaker the mass ____. In the sealed bag it ____. The difference is explained by ____.
frameChoices: The same reaction at two temperatures
The same reaction in two container sizes
coachPrompts: Was everything that ended up on the balance also on it at the start?
Is your difference bigger than your balance can actually resolve?
Could you convince someone who does not already believe you?

data.coachHint: Weigh the container too. Run it open and sealed.
data.sourceExcerpt: Do the same burning inside a sealed container and the total mass does not budge.
